facts.text: Levothyroxine sodium tablets are contraindicated in patients with uncorrected adrenal insufficiency.

Thyroid hormones, including levothyroxine, must not be used for obesity treatment or weight loss; doses beyond physiological replacement can cause life‑threatening toxicity, especially when combined with sympathomimetic (anorectic) agents.
Over‑ or under‑treatment can adversely affect growth, development, cardiovascular function, bone metabolism, reproductive function, cognition, gastrointestinal function, and glucose/lipid metabolism.

Elderly patients and those with underlying cardiovascular disease are at increased risk of cardiac adverse reactions (e.g., atrial fibrillation, angina, arrhythmias). Initiate therapy at lower than full replacement doses and monitor closely.
facts.population: Elderly and patients with cardiovascular disease

facts.text: Levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma; intravenous thyroid hormone formulations are required.
In patients with adrenal insufficiency, initiating levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement can precipitate acute adrenal crisis.
Levothyroxine therapy may worsen glycemic control in diabetes mellitus, potentially increasing insulin or antidiabetic drug requirements.
Over‑replacement can decrease bone mineral density, especially in post‑menopausal women, by increasing bone resorption.
facts.population: Post‑menopausal women and other patients at risk for osteoporosis

facts.text: The product contains FD&C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine), which may cause allergic reactions (including bronchial asthma) in susceptible individuals, particularly those with aspirin hypersensitivity.
Administer once daily on an empty stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast with a full glass of water; separate from interfering drugs by at least 4 hours.

Adult primary hypothyroidism: starting dose ≈1.6 µg/kg/day (full replacement). Titrate by 12.5–25 µg every 4–6 weeks based on serum TSH (or free‑T4 for secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism) until euthyroid.
Adults at risk for atrial fibrillation or with cardiac disease: start with a lower dose (<1.6 µg/kg/day) and titrate every 6–8 weeks.
Geriatric patients: initiate with a lower than full replacement dose (<1.6 µg/kg/day) and titrate slowly.

Pediatric dosing (per kg body weight): 0‑3 mo 10‑15 µg/kg/day; 3‑6 mo 8‑10 µg/kg/day; 6‑12 mo 6‑8 µg/kg/day; 1‑5 yr 5‑6 µg/kg/day; 6‑12 yr 4‑5 µg/kg/day; >12 yr (incomplete growth) 2‑3 µg/kg/day; >12 yr (complete growth) 1.6 µg/kg/day. Adjust every 2 weeks based on TSH/free‑T4.

Pregnant patients with pre‑existing hypothyroidism: increase dose by 12.5–25 µg/day once pregnancy is confirmed; monitor TSH each trimester and adjust to keep TSH within trimester‑specific reference range. Reduce to pre‑pregnancy dose after delivery.
Soybean flour, cottonseed meal, walnuts, and high‑fiber foods bind levothyroxine and decrease its absorption; grapefruit juice may delay absorption and reduce bioavailability.
Concomitant sympathomimetic (anorectic) agents increase risk of severe toxicity when levothyroxine is taken in supratherapeutic doses.
Thyroid hormone accelerates glucocorticoid clearance; glucocorticoid replacement should precede levothyroxine initiation in adrenal‑insufficient patients.

Changes in thyroxine‑binding globulin (TBG) affect interpretation of total T4/T3 assays; conditions that increase TBG (pregnancy, estrogen therapy, acute intermittent porphyria) raise total hormone levels, while conditions that decrease TBG (nephrosis, severe hypoproteinemia, severe liver disease, acromegaly, androgens, corticosteroids) lower them. Measure free‑T4 or calculate free‑T4 index when TBG is abnormal.
Nephrosis decreases TBG concentration, which can lower total T4/T3 levels and complicate laboratory monitoring of levothyroxine therapy.
